suggestions.title: 1. The body's warning signs: said in two places?
suggestions.question:
Your Risk of Harm paragraph says "If their body is flashing warning signs like severe overheating (not just regular sweating), severe insomnia, or trouble breathing ... reach out", and the Call medics list just above it has "Trouble breathing, blue or gray lips, or respiratory depression" and "Dangerous overheating, severe rigidity, or clonus with fever". How each option would read:

A (my pick): both stay as they are. Your paragraph says when to reach out at all; the list says which signs need an ambulance, with what your examples don't have (blue or gray lips, slow breathing, rigid muscles, jerking muscles with a fever). Pro: no safety sign is lost. Con: overheating and trouble breathing show up twice, a few lines apart.

B: the list keeps only what your paragraph doesn't say: "Blue or gray lips, or respiratory depression" and "Severe rigidity, or clonus with fever". Pro: each sign is said once. Con: someone scanning the list for when to call medics won't find "trouble breathing" or "overheating" there.
suggestions.why: You asked that the reasons to get urgent help be said only once. This is the one overlap I didn't cut myself, since cutting either side loses something a reader acts on in an emergency.
suggestions.advice_note: A, fairly sure: the list is where people look in an emergency, and your examples are why to reach out.

suggestions.title: 2. Recent Oral Toxic Ingestion: what to do when someone swallowed too much
suggestions.reading: The whole section in the first batch: [AI Generated, 100%](https://www.pangram.com/history/bb092688-faa8-46b1-9b14-b124951061eb).
suggestions.tested:
Your Risk of Harm moves carried in my words (the point and its bar first, plain words with the term in an aside, "etc." for the rest of the list, the reader's own judgment), each paragraph checked by itself:

1. "Before you pick a remedy for an "overdose", find out what they actually swallowed, how much and when, because that word alone doesn't tell you much. Then look at what their body is doing. ...": [AI Generated, 100%](https://www.pangram.com/history/1ed58643-6c98-4d83-b332-e610947a03e1).

2. The charcoal paragraph: [AI Generated, 100%](https://www.pangram.com/history/b822edbf-12eb-484e-a059-e0fbbc2a4f65).

3. The poison control paragraph: [AI Generated, 100%](https://www.pangram.com/history/c4970058-7666-4483-ad93-79165d24f15a).

The 911 line in Risk of Harm, said the same way, read the same: [AI Generated, 100%](https://www.pangram.com/history/45f31361-e5f6-4f1f-ace2-9a70cf644649).
suggestions.sense: A fresh reader of my version needed each step (what was swallowed, the body's state, when charcoal helps and when it's dangerous, when poison control is worth it) and flagged only the heading, the source link's label and my last line as ones a reader could lose. The guide's first paragraph asks the reader to sort the body into ten clinical states ("respiratory depression, stimulant toxicity, serotonin toxicity, ... objective neurological dysfunction ..."), most of which they can't name in the moment.
suggestions.why: Its shape, what to find out and what to do in a medical moment, said in clinical terms, is the medical part's other common shape: Acute Medical and Neurological Rescue, Suspected Serotonin Syndrome, Chest Pain's branch line and Active Seizure's first part all read AI in the first batch. Your Risk of Harm version taught me the firm list; this one is calmer, "find out, then decide", and my words in your frame still read AI.
suggestions.advice_note: Edit it: say what you'd tell someone whose friend swallowed too much of something, in your words. Keep the steps that keep them safe (charcoal only when they can swallow safely, never when they're vomiting, sedated or seizing), or tell me which can go. I'll carry what you do to the sections named above, test each, and put the ones that read Human straight in.
